title: Group acceptance - two approaches and one omission - 18 Nov
instructions: Explain how a university registration system should handle two students simultaneously requesting the last seat. Discuss transactions, duplicate prevention, and the benefits and risks of caching. This is a theoretical answer, not a coding task.
criteria: Distinguish duplicate enrollment from capacity concurrency
professional_rubric:
Assess theoretical understanding. A valid conceptual explanation suffices; do not require SQL code, every listed alternative, or topics outside the selected criterion. Separate independent criteria. An explicitly false claim is incorrect, not just missing coverage.

Correct atomicity and rollback
Atomicity groups the enrollment write and seat-count update as one all-or-nothing unit. If either fails, rollback undoes all changes in that transaction. Atomicity is distinct from isolation and capacity-race protection.
Valid solutions: A transaction encompassing both changes, committing together on success and rolling back both on any failure.; An equivalent conceptual all-or-nothing operation with explicit failure reversal.
Credit explicit transaction grouping plus rollback without requiring the word atomicity or an isolation-level name. Evaluate cache safety and concurrent capacity reservation in their own criteria; neither substitutes for nor negates an otherwise correct description of rollback.

Distinguish duplicate enrollment from capacity concurrency
Duplicate enrollment means the same student enrolling in the same course twice. Capacity concurrency means different students competing for limited seats. A UNIQUE key on the pair (student, course) rejects a repeated pair; different students form different pairs, so this key alone cannot enforce a course-wide capacity bound.
Valid solutions: Explicitly distinguish the per-student duplicate key from a separate shared-capacity reservation rule.; Explain that duplicate prevention and last-seat concurrency need distinct protections, even when both are used inside a transaction.
Judge the actual meaning of a claimed guarantee, not just the presence of UNIQUE or transaction keywords. A claim that a student/course uniqueness key prevents different students taking the final seat is technically incorrect.

Concrete protection against overbooking
A correct reservation must atomically check and consume shared remaining capacity under concurrent requests. Plain transaction grouping or per-student uniqueness alone does not make the capacity check safe. Separate reads followed by updates can race unless protected.
Valid solutions: Within the enrollment transaction, a conditional capacity update succeeds only while remaining seats are positive; accept enrollment only when it succeeds, and roll back on later failure.; Hold an exclusive lock on the shared course-capacity record inside the transaction, then recheck capacity, consume a seat and create enrollment before commit.; Serializable processing with correct handling/retry of serialization conflicts, or an equivalent explicitly explained atomic capacity reservation.
Any one sound approach is sufficient. Do not demand locks if a valid conditional update is given, or vice versa. A cache availability check, an unprotected database recheck, an ordinary transaction or a per-student UNIQUE key does not alone prove safe shared-capacity reservation.

Cache latency versus staleness trade-off
Caching can reduce read latency but cached seat availability can be stale. Cached availability may be a display hint; authoritative enrollment decisions must be validated against database state, with capacity concurrency handled by the separate reservation criterion.
Valid solutions: Explain faster cached reads and stale-data risk, with a final database validation instead of trusting cached availability alone.; Equivalent separation of cached display/read optimization and authoritative database enrollment decisions, with appropriate invalidation or freshness handling.
A policy accepting enrollment solely because the cache reports a free seat is explicitly wrong, not merely an omitted discussion. A final database check resolves the cache-trust issue but does not automatically satisfy atomicity or safe concurrent capacity reservation.

works.text: I handle two different students competing for the final course seat. I put the seat-count change and the enrollment insert in one database transaction. I use a conditional update: UPDATE courses SET remaining = remaining - 1 WHERE course_id = ? AND remaining > 0. Only one affected row means that this request reserved a seat. Zero affected rows means no seat was reserved, so I reject the request. I then insert enrollment and commit the two changes together. If the insert or either operation fails, I roll back every change in this transaction, including the reserved seat. I do not use an explicit SELECT FOR UPDATE lock; the successful conditional write protects the shared capacity. Cached availability makes browsing faster but can be stale. Cached values never authorize enrollment: the database conditional update is the final authority.

I start a transaction and acquire an exclusive lock on the shared course-capacity row using SELECT FOR UPDATE. After acquiring that lock, I recheck remaining seats. If no seats remain, I reject enrollment and roll back. Otherwise I decrement the seat count and insert enrollment while holding the lock, then commit both writes together. If either write fails, I roll back all changes in that transaction. A second student waits for the lock and then reads the updated capacity; if the first student took the last seat, the second sees zero and is rejected. My capacity mechanism is the exclusive row lock followed by a fresh check, rather than a conditional UPDATE WHERE remaining > 0. Separately, a UNIQUE constraint on (student_id, course_id) rejects repeated enrollment by the same student in the same course. Different students have different pairs, so this UNIQUE constraint does not protect the last shared seat; the row lock does. Cached counts make browsing faster but may be stale. Final enrollment uses the fresh locked database check, never cached availability.
